take_homes: A flat score tells me about the judge, not the work. A judge that checks only grounding stops finding things while the work can still get better.
A judge that never gets checked is a guess. Score a handful of outputs by hand next to it before I trust it. I never did this.
Floor and ceiling are two different evals. I have the floor and no ceiling for our non-engineering outputs.

monday.move: Hand-score about 10 outputs from our existing judge and compare with its verdicts. Then write a first steering judge for the sales team's internal update mails.
monday.who: me, with one engineer to set it up and one person from sales to say what good means
monday.stop_condition: If my verdicts match the judge on 8 of 10, I trust it for now. If not, I fix the judge before building anything on top of it.
monday.blocker: Nobody in sales has said what a good update mail is, and nobody owns the judge file after I write it.

misconception.why: I still think good agents mean good output, and I still skip review steps that look like ceremony. But 'nothing scores the judge' and 'every clean week erodes your ability to tell when the loop stops' hit my habit. Checking looks different when it's about the judge and not each output, so I'd count it as engineering, not beginner stuff. Not changed until I actually do the hand-scoring.

one_line: The first half repeats what my engineers already do, but 'a flat score is about the judge' and 'nobody checks the judge' are worth the hour, so I'd send a peer who skips review steps.
